COMPARED TO Rusty-margined Flycatcher (Myiozetetes cayanensis) is medium-size, perching bird in the Tyrant Flycatchers (Tyrannidae) family. Rusty-margined Flycatchers have a short bill. Bill is shorter than similar-looking Great Kiskadee (Pitangus sulphuratus). ""Rusty-margined is bright yellow below, with bold black-and-white head pattern. It is most similar to Social and White-ringed Flycatchers; look for combination of black cheek (not gray) and the obvious rufous in the wings. It has shorter bill than White-ringed. Voice is helpful: listen for lazy-sounding, slightly burry “wheeer” call. It is found in a variety of open wooded habitats such as forest edge and second growth, often around water in northern and central South America in Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, French Guiana, Guyana, Peru, Suriname, Venezuela and eastern Panama. Its natural habitats are subtropical or tropical moist lowland forests and heavily degraded former forest."" 5153013564				https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/	2025-08-13T12:12:00Z		https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/242223729	Irene					iNaturalist	Observations	iNaturalist research-grade observations		HumanObservation				https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/242223729	242223729		Irene					male	adult				alive														Buff-winged Starfrontlet (Coeligena lutetiae) is a species of hummingbird in the Trochilidae family. It is 11.4 cm (4.5 inches) long and is found in Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru. Buff-colored tertials on wings are conspicuous in flight and at rest, on both sexes. Male upperparts are velvety black; female upperparts are green. Adult female has buff throat; male has bluish-lilac throat. Its natural habitat is humid and wet upper montane forests and forest edges at elevation 2600-3600m (up to 11,800 ft). It is also know as Inca Galoneado in Spanish. Birds of Colombia, by Steven L. Hilty, March, 2021 (excellent color illustrations, species distribution maps, QR codes), p. 93. Ebird Checklist (#9 in list) with more photos: https://ebird.org/checklist/S191402450 xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Irene's Hummingbirds (Trochilidae family) observations on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=any&taxon_id=5562&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any Hummingbirds and Flowers: an INaturalist Project: https://www.inaturalist.org/projects/hummingbirds-and-flowers Did you know that hummingbirds . . . Are the smallest migrating birds. Their average weight is less than a nickel. Get their name from the humming sounds their wings make. Can perch, but cannot hop nor walk on their tiny legs. Have no sense of smell, but have excellent color vision. Can consume nectar up to twice their body weight in a day. In a flock may be called a bouquet, hover, glittering, shimmer or tune. Hummingbird Feeders: In addition to planting native plants for nectar, you can supplement hummingbird diet with a hummingbird feeder. 4:1 (or even 3:1) is a good ratio of water to sugar. Change the solution at least weekly before it gets cloudy or moldy, and NEVER add red dye! 5104304657				https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/	2025-04-06T22:17:15Z		https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/234249427	Irene					iNaturalist	Observations	iNaturalist research-grade observations		HumanObservation				https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/234249427	234249427		Irene							flowers																	Flowering Heliconia in San Peregrino, Manizales, Caldas, Colombia My favorite Heliconias (Genus Heliconia) observations: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=84964&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any Heliconias (Genus Heliconia) Common names for the genus include Lobster-claws, Toucan beak, Wild plantain, or False bird-of-paradise. Heliconias range from 0.5 to nearly 4.5 m (1.5–15 ft) tall, depending on the species. The simple leaves of these plants are 15–300 cm (6 in–10 ft) long. They are characteristically long, oblong, alternate, or growing opposite one another on nonwoody petioles often longer than the leaf, often forming large clumps with age. The leaves in different positions on the plant have a different absorption potential of sunlight for photosynthesis when exposed to different degrees of sunlight. They also look like lobster claws. Flowers are produced on long, erect or drooping panicles, and consist of brightly colored, waxy bracts, with small true flowers peeping out from the bracts. The growth habit of heliconias is similar to Canna, Strelitzia, and bananas, to which they are related. The flowers can be hues of reds, oranges, yellows, and greens, and are subtended by brightly colored bracts. The flowers' shape often limits pollination to a subset of the hummingbirds in the region. They also produce ample nectar that attract these birds. Fruits are blue-purple when ripe and primarily bird dispersed. https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/84964-Heliconia Plant Identification Terminology: An Illustrated Glossary, 2nd ed., by James Harris and M. It has crisp black-and-white barred back, dingy whitish face and underparts. Male has red crown and nape. Female has paler yellow-orange patch on nape only. Both sexes drum. There are several subspecies. Birds of Colombia, Steven L. Hilty, March, 2021 (excellent index, color illustrations, species distribution maps, QR codes), p. 237 Red-crowned Woodpecker ""is 16 to 18.5 cm (6.3 to 7.3 inches) long. The sexes' plumage is alike except for their head pattern. Adult males of the nominate subspecies have a pale yellow to whitish forehead, a bright red crown, and an orange-red nape and hindneck. Adult females have the same pale yellow to whitish forehead but a pale gray-buff to whitish crown and a reddish to orange-red nape and hindneck. Both sexes' cheeks, chin, and throat are grayish-buff. Their mantle and back are barred black and white and the rump and uppertail coverts are unbarred white. Their flight feathers are black with white bars throughout. Their tail is black with white bars on the central and outermost pairs of feathers. Their underparts are variable but usually buffish-gray to gray-buff with an olive or yellowish wash and a reddish to orange-red patch on the central belly. Their lower flanks and undertail coverts have black bars. Their bill is longish and blackish, their iris is red to brown, the bare skin around the eye gray-brown, and the legs gray. Juveniles are duller and browner than adults, their nape and hindneck are paler, their upperparts' bars less contrasting, their underparts often lightly streaked, and their belly patch paler and somewhat mottled."" Angehr and Robert. Dean, 2010 (excellent illustrations), p.178 ""Woodpeckers (Picidae) are found throughout much of the world (although not in Australasia). They are well adapted for drilling in wood, with strong, straight, chisel-like bills, grasping feet, and (except for the piculets) have stiffened tail feathers that serve as props for hitching up tree trunks and branches. Woodpeckers feed mainly on wood-boring insects, but some may also take ants from the ground or pick off flying insects. Some also consume fruit at bird feeders (or nuts in the case of the Acorn Woodpeckers). They can often be located by the tapping noise they make as they search for food; some also drum loudly as a territorial announcement. Woodpeckers nest in tree holes they excavate. These holes are often later used by other species of hole-nesting birds.” Woodpeckers of the World: an INaturalist Project: https://www.inaturalist.org/projects/woodpeckers-of-the-world Ebird with species description, range map and sound recordings: https://ebird.org/explore National Geographic Field Guide to the Birds of North America, ed. Birds of the World: https://birdsoftheworld.org/bow/species/piprid1/cur/introduction Manakins (Pipridae) family ""are small Neotropical passerines defined by compact bodies, short tails, broad-based bills, and extremely modified wing and leg musculature used for display rather than long-distance flight. Males show strong sexual dimorphism, with vivid plumage and elaborate courtship behaviors, while females are uniformly greenish and handle all nesting duties. Their most distinctive anatomical feature is the specialized wing structure that allows mechanical sound production: modified primaries, reinforced shafts, and hypertrophied wing muscles generate nonvocal snaps, pops, buzzes, and whirs during display flights. In species such as Manacus, rapid wing‑flicks produce sharp, explosive snaps created by the collision of the wings above the back, while Machaeropterus species use a single thickened primary to create a loud, percussive “snap” or “tick” as the feather vibrates. These sounds function in mate attraction and male–male competition and are often louder and more conspicuous than the birds’ vocalizations. Manakins exhibit acrobatic display jumps and rapid, precise movements enabled by unusually fast muscle contraction speeds. These characteristics make the family one of the most behaviorally specialized groups of Neotropical birds.” Birds of the World: Comprehensive life histories for all bird species and families (worldwide): Cornell Lab: https://birdsoftheworld.org/bow/home?__hstc= Ebird with species description, range map and sound recordings: https://ebird.org/explore Xeno-canto: Bird songs, sound recordings, bird range and migration map: https://xeno-canto.org/about/xeno-canto National Geographic Field Guide to the Birds of North America, ed. Flowerpiercers get their name from the fact that they have a sharp hook on the tip of their upper mandible which they use to slice open the base of flowers to get at the nectar. Birds of Colombia, by Steven L. Hilty, March, 2021 (excellent color illustrations, species distribution maps, QR codes,) p. 533. Xeno-canto: Bird songs, sound recordings, bird range and migration map: https://xeno-canto.org/species/Diglossa-lafresnayii Tanagers (Thraupidae) family is a huge and diverse family of neotropical birds that are undergoing dramatic taxonomic revisions based on emerging DNA data. Many new name changes are to come. Thraupidae have greatly varying bill shapes and sizes. Thraupidae currently includes Tanagers, Dacnis, Honeycreepers, some Seedeaters, some Finches, Saltators, and the Bananaquit. Thraupidae are mostly brightly colored, fruit-eating birds that will come to fruit feeders. They particularly like ripe bananas and papaya. ""They are often brightly colored, but some species are black and white. Males are typically more brightly colored than females and juveniles. Most have short, rounded wings. Most species are endemic to a relatively small area. Most live in pairs or in small groups of three to five individuals, often parents and their offspring."" Birds of Colombia, Steven L. Hilty, 2021, p. 505. 4954556898				https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/	2024-11-09T18:40:29Z		https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/247198544	Irene					iNaturalist	Observations	iNaturalist research-grade observations		HumanObservation				https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/247198544	247198544		Irene						adult				alive														Masked Flowerpiercer (Diglossa cyanea) is a blue neotropical perching bird in the Tanagers (Thraupidae) family. Adults are 15cm (6 inches) long and brighter blue than other Diglossa. It has a large, black, well-defined black mask and red eyes. Flowerpiercers get their name from the fact that they have a sharp hook on the tip of their upper mandible which they use to slice open the base of flowers to get at the nectar. Xeno-canto: Bird songs, sound recordings, bird range and migration map: https://xeno-canto.org/species/Diglossa-cyanea My favorite observations of Masked Flowerpiercer: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/247184519 xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Irene's Tanagers and Allies (Thraupidae) family observations on INaturalist: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=any&taxon_id=71369&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any Tanagers and Allies (Thraupidae) family is a very large and diverse family of neotropical birds that are undergoing dramatic taxonomic revisions based on emerging DNA data. Many new name changes are to come. Thraupidae are restricted to the Western Hemisphere and mainly to the tropics. About 60% live in South America, and 30% of these species live in the Andes. Many species are endemic to a relatively small area. Thraupidae family currently includes Tanagers, Dacnis, Honeycreepers, some Seedeaters, some Finches, Saltators, and the Bananaquit. Most have short, rounded wings and greatly varying bill shapes and sizes depending on the species' foraging habits. Many of the Tanagers are brightly colored, fruit-eating birds that will come to fruit feeders. They particularly like ripe bananas and papaya. Most tanagers live in pairs or in small groups of three to five individuals. These groups may consist simply of parents and their offspring. These birds may also be seen in single-species or mixed flocks. https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/71369-Thraupidae Birds of Colombia, Steven L. Hilty, 2021, pp. 505-552. 4954457835				https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/	2024-10-13T22:12:27Z		https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/247203006	Irene					iNaturalist	Observations	iNaturalist research-grade observations		HumanObservation				https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/247203006	247203006		Irene						adult				alive														"Crescent-faced Antpitta (Grallaricula lineifrons) is a rare, high-elevation, perching bird in the Antpittas (Grallariidae) family that looks like an ""egg on legs."" It is 12 cm (less than 5 inches) long with virtually no tail. It has a bold white-turning-to-pale yellow facial crescent under the large dark eye and heavily streaked underparts all the way to the tail. It is found in wet, mossy undergrowth at elevation 2800-3700m high in the Andes. Birds of Colombia, by Steven L. Ebird checklist (#12 in list): https://ebird.org/checklist/S191402450 Many confirmed observations of Crescent-faced Antpitta at this location: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/45015590 Crescent-faced Antpitta ""is found in Colombia and Ecuador. Its natural habitat is subtropical or tropical moist montane forest. It is becoming rare due to habitat loss and land fragmentation. It is one of the most strikingly plumaged members of the genus, perhaps even of the entire Grallariidae family. There is no recorded geographic variation within the limited range of this species. Adults are dark brown above with a slate-gray crown and nape, a bold white crescent in front of the eye, and densely streaked buff to whitish underparts. Almost nothing is known of the biology of this species, which currently is considered Near Threatened due to ongoing habitat fragmentation. Although the type specimen was collected in northeastern Ecuador in 1923, the Crescent-faced Antpitta remained unknown in life until nearly 50 years later. Today, based on regular reports and sightings by tourists and researchers, it is known to be more widespread than was previously thought, inhabiting the undergrowth of humid forests at elevations around 3,000 m. Its known distribution is nevertheless somewhat patchy, extending from southern Colombia to southern Ecuador along the eastern slope of the Andes. Only recently, 90 years after its formal description, was breeding of the Crescent-faced Antpitta reported in the literature, based on a single nest found very close to the type locality in northeastern Ecuador."" Found in montane forests at higher elevations than other quail-doves, from 1,000–3,300 m. Usually walks on the ground unless flushed up into the lower levels of a tree. Like most quail-doves, often best seen by quietly walking along trails at dawn and dusk. Listen for low-pitched descending “coo” notes."" 4954248664				https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/	2024-10-15T00:40:09Z		https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/233636717	Irene					iNaturalist	Observations	iNaturalist research-grade observations		HumanObservation				https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/233636717	233636717		Irene						adult				alive														"“Egg on Legs” and cute as a button. Crescent-faced Antpitta (Grallaricula lineifrons) is a rare, high-elevation, perching bird in the Antpittas (Grallariidae) family that looks like an ""egg on legs."" It is 12 cm (less than 5 inches) long with virtually no tail. It has a bold white-turning-to-pale yellow facial crescent under the large dark eye and heavily streaked underparts all the way to the tail. It is found in wet, mossy undergrowth at elevation 2800-3700m high in the Andes. Birds of Colombia, by Steven L. Hilty, March, 2021 (excellent color illustrations, species distribution maps, QR codes), p. 299. Ebird checklist (#12 in list): https://ebird.org/checklist/S191402450 Many confirmed observations of Crescent-faced Antpitta at this location: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/45015590 Crescent-faced Antpitta ""is found in Colombia and Ecuador. Its natural habitat is subtropical or tropical moist montane forest. It is becoming rare due to habitat loss and land fragmentation. It is one of the most strikingly plumaged members of the genus, perhaps even of the entire Grallariidae family. There is no recorded geographic variation within the limited range of this species. Adults are dark brown above with a slate-gray crown and nape, a bold white crescent in front of the eye, and densely streaked buff to whitish underparts. Almost nothing is known of the biology of this species, which currently is considered Near Threatened due to ongoing habitat fragmentation. Although the type specimen was collected in northeastern Ecuador in 1923, the Crescent-faced Antpitta remained unknown in life until nearly 50 years later. Today, based on regular reports and sightings by tourists and researchers, it is known to be more widespread than was previously thought, inhabiting the undergrowth of humid forests at elevations around 3,000 m. Its known distribution is nevertheless somewhat patchy, extending from southern Colombia to southern Ecuador along the eastern slope of the Andes. Only recently, 90 years after its formal description, was breeding of the Crescent-faced Antpitta reported in the literature, based on a single nest found very close to the type locality in northeastern Ecuador."" 4945831840				https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/	2025-05-03T14:15:38Z		https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/234076251	Irene					iNaturalist	Observations	iNaturalist research-grade observations		HumanObservation				https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/234076251	234076251		Irene						adult				alive														"COMPARE 2 Squirrels: Both are in the Tree Squirrels (Sciurus) genus and Squirrels (Sciuridae) family: Red-tailed Squirrel (Sciurus granatensis) Variegated Squirrel (Sciurus variegatoides) xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx COMPARE Red-tailed Squirrel (Sciurus granatensis) is an arboreal rodent with a long, bushy tail in the Tree Squirrels (Sciurus) genus and Squirrels (Sciuridae) family. It is endemic to Central and South America. Their range includes northern Costa Rica, southern Venezuela, Columbia, Panama, and Ecuador. Animal Diversity Web (ADW): https://animaldiversity.org/accounts/Sciurus_granatensis/ ""Red-tailed squirrels are found in a variety of habitats. They are found in both tropical and seasonal forests, in close proximity to water, and in croplands close to human populations. They are primarily found in seasonal rainforests inhabiting lower forest layers. Red-tailed squirrels are medium-sized squirrels. Their color varies greatly across the range of the species, especially in different habitats. Their dorsal surface is often dark orange, but can range from dull yellow sprinkled with black to all black. Some varieties of red-tailed squirrels have a median, dorsal stripe. Their ventral color ranges from completely white to bright orange-rust. The well-furred tail is dull yellowish brown and may or may not include a black tip. The ventral tail varies from dark yellowish brown to black with a dark yellow edge. The chin and sides of the throat are dark colored with dark yellow highlights with a yellowish-brown ring surrounding the eyes. The winter coat color may vary slightly from the summer coat."" https://animaldiversity.org/accounts/Sciurus_granatensis/ xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx COMPARE TO Variegated Squirrel (Sciurus variegatoides) is an arboreal rodent with a long, bushy tail in the Tree Squirrels (Sciurus) genus and Squirrels (Sciuridae) family. ""It is diurnal and seldom descends to the ground. It spends the night in a nest it builds which is sometimes in a hole in a tree but more often is constructed of leaves and built in the fork of a branch close to the trunk. There are many subspecies. Animal Diversity Web (ADW): https://animaldiversity.org/accounts/Sciurus_variegatoides/ Variegated squirrels (Sciurus variegatoides) are found in North and Central America, from southern Chiapas, Mexico to Central Panama. It ""occupies both dry and wet tropical forests, but prefers open, arid environments. It is found in deciduous, semi-deciduous, and, at times, evergreen forest. It is frequently found in open woodland, scrubland, and plantations. It lives at elevations ranging from sea level to 2500 m. Variegated Squirrel is a large, long-tailed species of tree squirrel. Its pelage is shiny and bristly. The fourteen different subspecies exhibit a wide range of color and color pattern. Dorsally, the color ranges from blackish to reddish brown to yellowish-gray to white. On the underside, the color ranges from white to cinnamon-buff. The feet and sides of the body are pale gray or yellowish; the ears have a pale patch of fur on the outside. Different subspecies may have a combination of dorsal and lateral stripes and forehead patches or may be completely grizzled in coloration."" xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Irene's Squirrels (Sciuridae) family observations on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=45933&user_id=aparrot1 Squirrels (Sciuridae) family includes tree squirrels, ground squirrels (including chipmunks and prairie dogs, among others), and flying squirrels. 4936825282				https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/	2025-02-18T00:29:58Z		https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/238019915	Irene					iNaturalist	Observations	iNaturalist research-grade observations		HumanObservation			"{""evidenceOfPresence"":""organism""}"	https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/238019915	238019915		Irene						adult				alive														Andean Guan with small, red dewlap at Hacienda El Bosque feeder in Colombia at elevation 3,900 ft xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Comparison of 3 wild Guans in Colombia. All are large landfowl in the Guans, Chachalacas, and Curassows (Cracidae) family. Cauca Guan (Penelope perspicax) Andean Guan (Penelope montagnii) and Sickle-winged Guan (Chamaepetes goudotii) xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Cauca Guan (Penelope perspicax) is a large, endemic, arboreal, landfowl bird in the Guans, Chachalacas, and Curassows (Cracidae) family. It is Endemic to Colombia. It has a large red dewlap and is 74cm (29 inches) long. It is found in humid, montane forest borders, older second growth, at 1200 to 2200m. It is found at lower elevations and the red dewlap is larger than those of the Andean Guan, which is found at higher elevations. Conservation Status: Vulnerable (VU) (IUCN Red List). Link to 2 observations (by Irene) of Cauca Guan in forest near Pereira, Risaralda, in Colombia: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/233386316 and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/237997597 Ebird Checklist with more photos of Cauca Guan: https://ebird.org/checklist/S191402455 Birds of Colombia, by Steven L. Hilty, March, 2021 (excellent color illustrations, species distribution maps, QR codes,) p. 30. Found Feathers (Worldwide): https://www.fws.gov/lab/featheratlas/idtool.php Irene's Ebird Profile: https://ebird.org/profile/MTIwNjIzMg and my worldwide checklists: https://ebird.org/mychecklists xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx COMPARED TO Andean Guan (Penelope montagnii) is an arboreal landfowl in the Guans, Chachalacas, and Curassows (Cracidae) family and is 58cm (24 inches) long. The red dewlap is inconspicous (compared to prominent red dewlap of Cauca Guan). It is found in humid and wet montane forest, second growth, patches of woodland to treeline at 2200-3700m (higher elevations of the Andeas than Cuaca Guan). Link to Andean Guan observation at Hacienda El Bosque feeder in Colombia at elevation 3,900 ft: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/238019915 Ebird checklist with more Andean Guan photos at Hacienda El Bosque: https://ebird.org/checklist/S191402450 Birds of Colombia, by Steven L. Hilty, March, 2021 (excellent color illustrations, species distribution maps, QR codes,) p. 29. xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx COMPARED TO Sickle-winged Guan (Chamaepetes goudotii) is a large, endemic, arboreal, landfowl bird in the Guans, Chachalacas, and Curassows (Cracidae) family and is 51-64 cm (20-25 inches) long. It is found in humid and wet montane forest and older second growth at 800-3000m. It is rufous below and has NO dewlap. Male has bare, bright blue facial skin, less blue in females. Link to observation of FEMALE Sickle-winged Guan: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/238016565 Ebird Checklist at Hacienda El Bosque with more photos of both female and male: https://ebird.org/checklist/S191402450 Birds of Colombia, by Steven L. This one is female. xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Comparison of 3 wild Guans in Colombia. All are large landfowl in the Guans, Chachalacas, and Curassows (Cracidae) family. Cauca Guan (Penelope perspicax) Andean Guan (Penelope montagnii) and Sickle-winged Guan (Chamaepetes goudotii) xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Cauca Guan (Penelope perspicax) is a large, endemic, arboreal, landfowl bird in the Guans, Chachalacas, and Curassows (Cracidae) family. It is Endemic to Colombia. It has a large red dewlap and is 74cm (29 inches) long. It is found in humid, montane forest borders, older second growth, at 1200 to 2200m. It is found at lower elevations and the red dewlap is larger than those of the Andean Guan, which is found at higher elevations. Conservation Status: Vulnerable (VU) (IUCN Red List). Link to 2 observations (by Irene) of Cauca Guan in forest near Pereira, Risaralda, in Colombia: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/233386316 and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/237997597 Ebird Checklist with more photos of Cauca Guan: https://ebird.org/checklist/S191402455 Birds of Colombia, by Steven L. Hilty, March, 2021 (excellent color illustrations, species distribution maps, QR codes,) p. 30. Found Feathers (Worldwide): https://www.fws.gov/lab/featheratlas/idtool.php Irene's Ebird Profile: https://ebird.org/profile/MTIwNjIzMg and my worldwide checklists: https://ebird.org/mychecklists xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx COMPARED TO Andean Guan (Penelope montagnii) is an arboreal landfowl in the Guans, Chachalacas, and Curassows (Cracidae) family and is 58cm (24 inches) long. The red dewlap is inconspicous (compared to prominent red dewlap of Cauca Guan). It is found in humid and wet montane forest, second growth, patches of woodland to treeline at 2200-3700m (higher elevations of the Andeas than Cuaca Guan). Link to confirmed Andean Guan observation at Hacienda El Bosque feeder in Colombia at elevation 3,900 (?): https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/238019915 Ebird checklist with more Andean Guan photos at Hacienda El Bosque: https://ebird.org/checklist/S191402450 Birds of Colombia, by Steven L. Hilty, March, 2021 (excellent color illustrations, species distribution maps, QR codes,) p. 29. xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx COMPARED TO Sickle-winged Guan (Chamaepetes goudotii) is a large, endemic, arboreal, landfowl bird in the Guans, Chachalacas, and Curassows (Cracidae) family and is 51-64 cm (20-25 inches) long. It is found in humid and wet montane forest and older second growth at 800-3000m. It is rufous below and has NO dewlap. Male has bare, bright blue facial skin, less blue in females. Link to confirmed observation of FEMALE Sickle-winged Guan: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/238016565 Ebird Checklist at Hacienda El Bosque with more photos of both female and male: https://ebird.org/checklist/S191402450 Birds of Colombia, by Steven L. Tanagers (Thraupidae) family is a huge and diverse family of neotropical birds that are undergoing dramatic taxonomic revisions based on emerging DNA data. Many new name changes are to come. Thraupidae have greatly varying bill shapes and sizes. Thraupidae currently includes Tanagers, Dacnis, Honeycreepers, some Seedeaters, some Finches, Saltators, and the Bananaquit. Thraupidae are mostly brightly colored, fruit-eating birds that will come to fruit feeders. They particularly like ripe bananas and papaya. ""They are often brightly colored, but some species are black and white. Males are typically more brightly colored than females and juveniles. Most have short, rounded wings. Most species are endemic to a relatively small area. Most live in pairs or in small groups of three to five individuals, often parents and their offspring."" Birds of Colombia, Steven L. Hilty, 2021, p. 505. Leaves of melastomes are somewhat distinctive, being opposite, decussate, and usually with 3-7 longitudinal veins arising either from the base of the blade, plinerved (inner veins diverging above base of blade), or pinnately nerved with three or more pairs of primary veins diverging from the mid-vein at successive points above the base. Tanagers (Thraupidae) family is a huge and diverse family of neotropical birds that are undergoing dramatic taxonomic revisions based on emerging DNA data. Many new name changes are to come. Thraupidae have greatly varying bill shapes and sizes. Thraupidae currently includes Tanagers, Dacnis, Honeycreepers, some Seedeaters, some Finches, Saltators, and the Bananaquit. Thraupidae are mostly brightly colored, fruit-eating birds that will come to fruit feeders. They particularly like ripe bananas and papaya. ""They are often brightly colored, but some species are black and white. Males are typically more brightly colored than females and juveniles. Most have short, rounded wings. Most species are endemic to a relatively small area. Most live in pairs or in small groups of three to five individuals, often parents and their offspring."" Birds of Colombia, Steven L. Hilty, 2021, p. 505. This one is female. xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Comparison of 3 wild Guans in Colombia. All are large landfowl in the Guans, Chachalacas, and Curassows (Cracidae) family. Cauca Guan (Penelope perspicax) Andean Guan (Penelope montagnii) and Sickle-winged Guan (Chamaepetes goudotii) xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx Cauca Guan (Penelope perspicax) is a large, endemic, arboreal, landfowl bird in the Guans, Chachalacas, and Curassows (Cracidae) family. It is Endemic to Colombia. It has a large red dewlap and is 74cm (29 inches) long. It is found in humid, montane forest borders, older second growth, at 1200 to 2200m. It is found at lower elevations and the red dewlap is larger than those of the Andean Guan, which is found at higher elevations. Conservation Status: Vulnerable (VU) (IUCN Red List). Link to 2 observations (by Irene) of Cauca Guan in forest near Pereira, Risaralda, in Colombia: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/233386316 and https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/237997597 Ebird Checklist with more photos of Cauca Guan: https://ebird.org/checklist/S191402455 Birds of Colombia, by Steven L. Hilty, March, 2021 (excellent color illustrations, species distribution maps, QR codes,) p. 30. Found Feathers (Worldwide): https://www.fws.gov/lab/featheratlas/idtool.php Irene's Ebird Profile: https://ebird.org/profile/MTIwNjIzMg and my worldwide checklists: https://ebird.org/mychecklists xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx COMPARED TO Andean Guan (Penelope montagnii) is an arboreal landfowl in the Guans, Chachalacas, and Curassows (Cracidae) family and is 58cm (24 inches) long. The red dewlap is inconspicous (compared to prominent red dewlap of Cauca Guan). It is found in humid and wet montane forest, second growth, patches of woodland to treeline at 2200-3700m (higher elevations of the Andeas than Cuaca Guan). Link to Andean Guan observation at Hacienda El Bosque feeder in Colombia at elevation 3,900 (?): https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/238019915 Ebird checklist with more Andean Guan photos at Hacienda El Bosque: https://ebird.org/checklist/S191402450 Birds of Colombia, by Steven L. Hilty, March, 2021 (excellent color illustrations, species distribution maps, QR codes,) p. 29. xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx COMPARED TO Sickle-winged Guan (Chamaepetes goudotii) is a large, endemic, arboreal, landfowl bird in the Guans, Chachalacas, and Curassows (Cracidae) family and is 51-64 cm (20-25 inches) long. It is found in humid and wet montane forest and older second growth at 800-3000m. It is rufous below and has NO dewlap. Male has bare, bright blue facial skin, less blue in females. Link to observation of FEMALE Sickle-winged Guan: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/238016565 Ebird Checklist at Hacienda El Bosque with more photos of both female and male: https://ebird.org/checklist/S191402450 Birds of Colombia, by Steven L. Hilty, March, 2021 (excellent color illustrations, species distribution maps, QR codes,) p. 28. Tanagers (Thraupidae) family is a huge and diverse family of neotropical birds that are undergoing dramatic taxonomic revisions based on emerging DNA data. Many new name changes are to come. Thraupidae have greatly varying bill shapes and sizes. Thraupidae currently includes Tanagers, Dacnis, Honeycreepers, some Seedeaters, some Finches, Saltators, and the Bananaquit. Thraupidae are mostly brightly colored, fruit-eating birds that will come to fruit feeders. They particularly like ripe bananas and papaya. Most species are endemic to a relatively small area. Most live in pairs or in small groups of three to five individuals, often parents and their offspring."" Birds of Colombia, Steven L. 4921519135				https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/	2024-08-27T02:53:22Z		https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/234080349	Irene					iNaturalist	Observations	iNaturalist research-grade observations		HumanObservation				https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/234080349	234080349		Irene						adult				alive														"Birds of Colombia, by Steven L. Hilty, March, 2021 (excellent color illustrations, species distribution maps, QR codes,) Merlin Bird ID: How to use/get the portable App (Bird ID help for 8,500+ species) https://merlin.allaboutbirds.org/ Comprehensive Feather I.D. tools and more: https://foundfeathers.org/resources/ Found Feathers (Worldwide): https://www.fws.gov/lab/featheratlas/idtool.php Tanagers (Thraupidae) family has a Neotropical distribution and is the second-largest family of birds. It represents about 4% of all avian species and 12% of the Neotropical birds. They are mostly brightly colored fruit-eating birds. Tanagers are often brightly colored, but some species are black and white. Males are typically more brightly colored than females and juveniles. Most tanagers have short, rounded wings. The shape of the bill seems to be linked to the species' foraging habits. Tanagers are restricted to the Western Hemisphere and mainly to the tropics. About 60% of tanagers live in South America, and 30% of these species live in the Andes. Most species are endemic to a relatively small area. Most tanagers live in pairs or in small groups of three to five individuals. These groups may consist simply of parents and their offspring. These birds may also be seen in single-species or mixed flocks. Many tanagers are thought to have dull songs, though some are elaborate. Tanagers are omnivorous, and their diets vary by genus. They have been seen eating fruits, seeds, nectar, flower parts, and insects. Many pick insects off branches or from holes in the wood. Other species look for insects on the undersides of leaves. Yet others wait on branches until they see a flying insect and catch it in the air. Many of these particular species inhabit the same areas, but these specializations alleviate competition."" https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/71369-Thraupidae Irene's Ebird Profile: https://ebird.org/profile/MTIwNjIzMg and my worldwide checklists (including Colombia): https://ebird.org/mychecklists"															2024-08-05T08:19:01-05:00	08:19:01-05:00						2024-08-05 08:19:01-05:00																				CO	Caldas				La China, Manizales, Caldas, CO												5.0648166667	-75.5924216667	EPSG:4326																																			524072281				Irene		2024-08-06T03:33:33Z				979968								Stilpnia vitriolina								Animalia	Chordata	Aves	Passeriformes		Thraupidae				Stilpnia							species
